title: The Lord in every heart
hookLine: ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai: the Lord dwells in every heart, as the holy proclaim (Salok M9, ang 1427)

cards: Sikh tradition tells of a man named Bhai Ghanaiya. During the battles around Anandpur, he carried a water skin across the battlefield and gave water to the wounded, to Sikhs and to the soldiers they were fighting.

Some Sikhs were furious and brought him before Guru Gobind Singh. The Guru asked him why he was helping the enemy. Bhai Ghanaiya is remembered as answering that he saw no enemy: in every face, he saw only the Guru.
The Guru, the story says, gave him ointment as well, and told him to bandage their wounds too.

teach.b: His answer echoes today's salok, written by Guru Gobind Singh's own father. Ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai, santan kahio pukaar. In paraphrase: the Lord dwells in every heart; the holy ones have proclaimed it aloud.

Then: says Nanak, meditate on Him, O mind, and you'll cross the terrifying ocean. Ghatt means a clay pot, a vessel, and from that, the body or heart that holds a life. Ghatt ghatt: pot after pot, every single vessel.
Not just the devout or the kind, or our own people. Every vessel.

teach.h: PUKAAR: THE HOLY CALL IT ALOUD.
teach.b: And pukaar is a loud call, a shout: the holy haven't whispered this. Last week, in the forest hymn, the Lord was within like scent in a flower; that was about finding God inside yourself.
This salok turns the same teaching outward. Every vessel means mine, and yours, and the stranger's, and the soldier's on the other side. That's what makes it hard.
Seeing God in the people we love comes more easily. The salok doesn't stop there.
Sikhs see the same line at work in langar, which feeds anyone who walks in, of any faith or none, seated together on the floor.
Seva, service, isn't reserved for members either. And Bhai Ghanaiya's water skin is what the line looks like when someone lives it.

how: Sikhs serve langar to anyone who comes, seated together on the floor, and remember Bhai Ghanaiya, who gave water to the wounded on both sides, as a model of seeing the Lord in every heart.

o: a clay vessel, the heart or body
a water skin carried into battle

games.q: the Lord in every heart — tap the pairs.
p: a clay vessel, the heart or body

s: the salok says the Lord dwells only in the hearts of the devout
ghatt ghatt: every vessel, every heart.
Bhai Ghanaiya gave water to wounded soldiers on both sides
tradition says he saw only the Guru in every face.
the salok says the holy have kept this truth quiet
they have proclaimed it aloud, pukaar.

games.q: you're Guru Gobind Singh. a Sikh is brought before you for giving water to the enemy's wounded. what do you do?
o: punish him for helping the enemy.
ask why, then give him ointment for their wounds too.
games.why: tradition says Bhai Ghanaiya answered that he saw only the Guru in every face, and the Guru gave him ointment to bandage their wounds as well.

practice: Bring to mind one person you find difficult, not your worst enemy, just someone who annoys you or whom you've written off, and picture the salok's clay vessel.
You don't have to like them; let the thought sit, the Lord dwells here too, and notice what softens and what resists. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru for one breath.

wordCard.voice: Ghatt, a vessel, the heart. Ghatt ghatt mai har joo basai: the salok says the Lord lives in every ghatt, every heart, as the holy proclaim aloud.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ghatt, a clay pot, a vessel, and so the body or heart. Ghatt ghatt: in every one.

carryVoice: Your line: in every heart. Every heart includes the ones on the other side. That's day five hundred ninety-two.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 12 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427)
